newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to send six light tanks to Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: France to send six light tanks to Brazzaville.

text.p: France is to immediately reinforce its 1,250-strong army contingent in the embattled Congolese capital of Brazzaville with half a dozen light tanks, the army said on Thursday.
"We're sending in six ERC-90 Sagaies from the Foreign Legion's First Cavalry Regiment," a military spokesman told Reuters.
The Sagaie, designed for desert warfare, is equipped with a 90 mm cannon and used in reconnaissance units of French armoured divisions.

The tanks will give added firepower to French troops whose mission to protect and evacuate foreign nationals from bitter fighting between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and those of former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The French army has so far rescued and brought to Brazzaville airport some 2,954 people from 50 nationalities, the spokesman said.

Of these, 2,507 have been flown out of the city, mostly to Gabon, aboard French air force C-130 Hercules and C-160 Transalls in what the army described as "very difficult conditions". The evacuees included 1,282 French nationals.
The planes have been taking off and landing on an airstrip around which rival factions have clashed. The area where the evacuees were gathered came under fire on Wednesday.
Reports from Brazzaville said mortar blasts and grenade explosions echoed around areas near the airport early on Thursday despite a ceasefire called to end a week of fighting.
Brazzaville itself saw a few hours of quiet after Lissouba ordered his troops to stop firing on Wednesday afternoon and Sassou Nguesso urged his supporters to observe the ceasefire.
Shocked evacuees who arrived in Paris early on Wednesday spoke of "butchery" in the streets of Brazzaville.
Some said they barricaded themselves in their homes, but increasingly fell prey to roaming bands of armed looters, including some uniformed members of the government forces.
"In the end, we became afraid that after looting, they would start raping our wives and children so we decided to pull out," one man told French television.

One radio report quoted an evacuee as saying French soldiers on the spot told him there might be 10,000 dead in Brazzaville but military sources in Paris said they had no such figures and were wary of them.

One senior officer told Reuters in Paris: "We don't know how many have been killed. Because much of Brazzaville is made up of shantytowns where people live tightly packed, it is possible some rounds from multiple rockets launchers they are using may have caused heavy casualties in places.
"There could be 200 dead or 1,000 dead in the very worst case scenario but we don't know," he said.
The clashes began on June 5 after soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on militias and illegal arms ahead of a July 27 presidential election.
Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election after Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979, bowed to calls for multi-party politics.
Lissouba told the French daily newspaper Liberation in an interview published on Thursday that he did not know if the truce would hold. "If Sassou wants to continue the war, well, too bad."
